item.title: Shamash Alidina: Gratitude with Room for Everything Else
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: essential for this reader

Gratitude practices sometimes feel like one more thing to get right, as if we’re supposed to feel thankful on cue no matter what’s happening.

Our guest this week is Shamash Alidina. He offers a gentler approach. You make room for whatever you’re feeling, and then you see whether one small, ordinary thing you appreciate can sit alongside it.

In this meditation, you’ll:

- Acknowledge how life is for you right now

- Hold difficulty and appreciation side by side

- Connect gratitude to what you value, rather than just how you feel

Shamash Alidina: Gratitude with Room for Everything Else

Or listen to the guided audio.

- Find a comfortable position and let your body settle. You can close your eyes or keep them open with a soft, relaxed gaze. There’s nothing to achieve here. You don’t need to feel calm, happy, or grateful. You’re simply giving yourself a little time to be here.

- Notice the places where your body makes contact with what’s beneath you. Feel the gentle movement of your breath. There’s no need to change it. Just notice the body breathing in and breathing out.

- Allow whatever you’re experiencing to be here. Maybe your mind is busy or your body feels restless. That’s fine. There’s nothing you need to fix.

- Bring to mind how life is for you at the moment. Perhaps something is worrying you. Maybe you’re missing someone, feeling lonely, or facing a challenge. Or perhaps things are going reasonably well. Whatever you notice, acknowledge it honestly. You might silently say, This is what I’m experiencing right now.

- Notice any feeling in your body that comes with this experience. It might be tightness, heaviness, or restlessness. You don’t need to make it go away. Imagine making room for it the way you’d make room for a visitor at your door. You don’t have to invite it to stay forever. Just acknowledge that it’s here. For these few moments, there’s no need to talk yourself out of how you feel. Let yourself be a human being with human experiences.

- With the difficulty in the background, look for one small thing you appreciate. It might be someone who cares about you, a place where you feel safe, a warm drink, a comfortable bed, or a memory of laughter. Something quite ordinary is enough. If nothing comes to mind, that’s perfectly fine. Simply notice the support beneath your body or feel your feet on the floor. You don’t have to produce gratitude on demand.

- If you’ve found something, take a little time with it. What about this person, place, or experience matters to you? Maybe it brings warmth, comfort, connection, or relief. Maybe it’s simply pleasant. Don’t force the feeling to be bigger than it is.

- Notice the details. If it’s a memory, recall it gently. If it’s happening now, explore it through your senses. Let yourself receive the experience rather than hurrying on to the next thing.

- Hold both the difficult and the good. You don’t need to get rid of a difficult feeling to appreciate something good. You can feel worried and still enjoy being supported. You can feel sad and remember someone you love. You can feel lonely and appreciate a small, kind interaction. Imagine holding the difficulty in one hand and this small appreciation in the other.

- Consider what this moment of appreciation points toward. Is there something you value in it, such as connection, kindness, friendship, health, creativity, or a little space to stop and breathe? Is there one small action you could take today to bring more of it into your life? You could send someone a message, step outside, take a proper break, or offer yourself a little more patience. If today is hard, the kindest thing may be to allow yourself some rest or support. Gratitude doesn’t require you to pretend everything is fine.

- Return to your surroundings. Notice your breathing, the sounds around you, and the support beneath your body. When you’re ready, gently open your eyes if they’ve been closed, and bring some gentle movement into your body.

- Thank yourself for taking these few minutes. May you find room for both the difficult moments and the small moments of goodness in the days ahead.

item.title: You’re Not Too Much Just Because Someone Else Needs Less
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: strong, worth their time

“Being myself doesn’t give me unlimited access to somebody else’s attention.”

I am a talkative person.

Not “occasionally enjoys conversation” talkative. I can answer a question, take three side roads, remember something from 1987, and still believe I gave you the short version.

I’m also a helper. When I care about someone, I want to find exactly the right example to make something click. Unfortunately, I have a habit of continuing long after the click.

For years, I thought being myself meant showing up with all of that enthusiasm. Now I’m learning something so obvious I’m almost embarrassed it took me this long: the other person gets to be themselves too.

I learned that the hard way during my years working with foster children and families. I could get so excited about helping a young person understand something that I’d explain it from six directions. I was giving an excellent presentation, at least according to the person giving it.

On one occasion, a young person I cared about a lot told me I was using too many words.

Well, shit.

I was going full steam down one track with the backstory, the examples, the whole TED Talk. She wanted the movie trailer. She had asked me directly to stop beating around the bush.

My first reaction was confusion. What do you mean? This is good!

Then embarrassment. Then a much less flattering question: Was I still talking to help her, or was I partly entertaining myself?

I realized I had been trying to do everything at once: explain, soften the message, make it interesting, help her feel safe. Some of that was care.

But some of it, honestly, was fear. I didn’t fully trust that I could say something directly and let it be enough.

She had told me exactly what she needed in that moment—fewer words, not more. And caring about her meant honoring what she needed, even if it wasn’t how I naturally communicated.

So I regrouped and tried again. Not with a different personality. Just a different way of showing up for the person in front of me.

I wish I could say I always took that kind of feedback so well.

Other times, I ran the whole spectrum from martyr to victim in my head: Well, that’s the last time I ever try to help you. If I’m too much for you today, I must be too much for you forever. Maybe we shouldn’t even be friends since I can’t truly be me.

It’s quite a leap from “Can you get to the point?” to “Apparently I should retire my entire personality.” But I have made it.

And when I’m not very invested in the person, I’m more likely to just shut down. Pride and ego win, I detach, and I stop talking.

I’m not always known for taking redirection well. I am getting better.

Recently I heard about someone who kept talking to a woman during her workout. She wasn’t there to socialize; she wanted to concentrate on exercising. When the conversation didn’t go well, the response afterward was essentially, “Well, I have to be me.”

Yes. You do. But she gets to be her too.

That sentence has been rattling around in my head ever since. Because “I have to be me” sounds wonderful until being me requires somebody else to stop being themselves.

If I love talking, that doesn’t mean you have to love listening at that moment. If I process things aloud, you aren’t automatically my processing partner.

I can be enthusiastic, curious, funny, and capable of producing a twelve-minute answer to a question that technically required the word “yes.” Those things can all genuinely be me. But they still land somewhere.

Maybe you are tired, distracted, or simply finished with the conversation. I don’t need to decide which explanation is right before I respect it.

Sometimes we treat another person as a charging station. We come away from a long conversation feeling wonderful. We told the story, got the laugh, processed the problem.

Meanwhile, they may have been running on fourteen percent the whole time. Then they say they need quiet, and suddenly we’re the injured party.

Now the quieter person has two jobs. First, manage their own overload. Second, manage our feelings about the fact that they are overloaded.

But being asked for less conversation isn’t necessarily being asked to become less of a person. I can mean well and still overwhelm someone. And being myself doesn’t give me unlimited access to somebody else’s attention.

Maybe somebody really does think you are too much. That can hurt.

But before you turn that into a life sentence, add the missing words: Too much for whom? Too much when? Too much for what?

Maybe you are not too much for your best friend. Maybe you are too much while she is trying to exercise.

Maybe you are not too much for your partner. Maybe you are too much at 6:30 in the morning before coffee.

That is not a moral failure. It is information.

And it works both ways. One person may feel connected by talking everything through. Another may feel connected by sitting together without a word.

Neither one is broken.

These days I still love stories, jokes, metaphors, and the moment when someone’s face says, “I get it.” None of that needs to disappear.

But I’m trying to catch myself sooner when I stop noticing the person who has to receive all my wonderful information.

Sometimes the best thing I can do is ask, “Do you want the short version?”

And then, here’s the radical part: actually give it.

I don’t need to turn myself off. I can turn the volume down. The quieter person gets to be themselves, and I still get to be me.

About Kelly Blakey

Kelly Blakey is a writer, mother, and former social worker with thirty years of experience in behavioral health. Drawing from her professional and personal experiences, she writes about the patterns that shape our relationships, the stories we tell ourselves, and what happens when we begin questioning them. She is the author of Holy Shit, That’s Me and Holy Shit, I Do That Too. Visit her at HelpingHealer.com.

Source: Tiny Buddha | Published: 2026-11-25 16:19 UTC | Difficulty: 40/100

item.title: The Home Depot Is Giving Away Free Milwaukee, DeWalt, and Makita Cordless Power Tools for Black Friday
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, learning value

As anyone who has ever shopped at The Home Depot (or any hardware store) knows, power tools are expensive. That’s why Black Friday at The Home Depot is so important: It’s the perfect opportunity to get the tools you’ve been wanting at some pretty steep discounts. And the best deals even give you a free tool if you purchase a starter kit from one of the major tool brands (Ryobi, DeWalt, Makita, or Milwaukee).

Get a free cordless power tool after buying a Ryobi, DeWalt, Makita, or Milwaukee starter kit

Here’s how this year's “buy one, get one” (BOGO) deal works: Pick out a starter kit from one of the brands, add it to your cart, and you’ll be presented with a list of available tools you can add (they’ll be marked “FREE,” so you can’t get confused). When you go to check out, the price of the tool will be listed as “SAVINGS.”

Here are the starter kits you can choose from:

- Ryobi ONE+ 18V Starter Kit (includes one 4.0Ah and one 2.0Ah battery and charger). Cost: $99.

- DeWalt 20V Max Starter Kit (includes 6.0Ah and 4.0Ah batteries and charger). Cost: $199.

- Makita 18V LXT Starter Pack (includes two 5.0Ah batteries and a rapid charger). Cost: $199.

- Milwaukee M18 FUEL Combo Kit (includes a brushless, cordless hammer drill and an impact driver). Cost: $399.

Note that the Ryobi, DeWalt, and Milwaukee offers include 14 free tools to choose from, while the Makita offer only includes 8. Also, note that while the Ryobi starter kit is your cheapest option for a free tool, the batteries included are weaker. The DeWalt or Makita batteries cost more, but offer more power and flexibility.

Some of the deals go beyond just getting a freebie. For example, if you choose the DeWalt Starter Kit for $199, you can get an Atomic 20V Max impact wrench that normally costs $239 for free, which is a significant savings even if you already have batteries and a charger and don’t really need those items (plus, you can never have too many batteries).

The Home Depot's best Black Friday tool deals

The Home Depot is also offering deep discounts on just about everything in the store. Some of the most notable tool deals include:

- 50% off this DeWalt Cordless Brushless Oscillating Multi Tool, including battery and charger

- 33% off this Ryobi Combo Kit, an incredible deal for a circular saw, reciprocating saw, and a power drill/driver plus two batteries and a charger; the batteries are small, but this is a great deal on a starter kit.

- 42% off this Combo Kit from Milwaukee, including a Packout toolbox, a hammer drill, an impact driver, a grinder, and a reciprocating saw, plus two batteries and a charger—a massive deal for anyone who needs to tool up rapidly.

- 45% off this Brushless Cordless Impact Wrench Kit from Ryobi, which includes a battery and charger.

That only scratches the surface—if you’ve ever needed anything from Home Depot, Black Friday is the day to run out and get it.

Tips for shopping The Home Depot Black Friday sale

Of course, Black Friday can be a little chaotic, so here are a few tips to maximize your savings and experience:

- Check online and in-store. Some deals are in-store only, and some items (especially BOGO tools) may not be available at your nearest location—make sure you enter your ZIP code when you’re checking out to ensure you won’t have any problems.

- Consider whether you need more batteries and chargers. Depending on your existing collection of batteries and chargers, buying more to get the discount may or may not make sense.

- There's no price matching or rain checks. Remember that the store won’t honor price-matching or offer rain checks on Black Friday items.

- Cyber Monday will have deals, too. More deals will be rolled out on Cyber Monday (November 30), which may include items you want but don’t see on sale for Black Friday. But keep in mind that Black Friday prices probably won’t go any lower—so snap up what you need as soon as you can.

- Sign up for text alerts to save a little more. Home Depot offers a $5 coupon (off a purchase of $50 or more) when you sign up for email or text alerts, which you may be able to apply to your Black Friday purchase for a little extra savings.

If you can’t find what you need at The Home Depot

Home Depot isn’t the only store offering free tool giveaways:

- Like Home Depot, Lowes is offering BOGO tools with the purchase of starter kits from major tool brands.

- Tractor Supply Co. has a wide range of BOGO tool offers during its Black Friday Event.

- If you’re looking for outdoor equipment, note that Bass Pro Shops and Cabela’s aren’t offering a BOGO deal this year, but the first 250 customers at each physical store will receive a free “mystery promo card” valued between $10 and $500. If you’re going to go for this, plan to line up early—250 cards are going to go fast.

Black Friday FAQs

Who has the best deals on tools right now?

The best early deals on tools right now are at Home Depot, where you can get up to 65% off on select Milwaukee tools, 50% off on DeWalt tools, and 30% off on Ryobi tools. They also have several offers for over 50% off on hand tools..

Who has better prices on tools, Lowes or Home Depot?

Home Depot and Lowe’s often compete with each other for seasonal sales, so it’s always a good idea to check both sites before buying. Right now, Home Depot has the best deals on DeWalt and Milwaukee cordless tool sets, but Lowe’s has a better deal on Craftsman hand tool sets.

What is the best time of year to buy tools?

The best prices of the year on tools are during the holidays in November and December. This is because of the holiday shopping push, as well as making space for new tools that come out in the spring. The second-best time to buy tools is in May and June during Father’s Day sales.

Source: Lifehacker | Published: 2026-11-25 20:45 UTC | Difficulty: 40/100

item.title: Beats' Newest Over-Ear Headphones Are Down to a Record-Low $249 for Black Friday
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, learning value

While you can find plenty of deals on older headphone models during Black Friday sales, it’s rare to see a record-low price and a nearly 30% discount on newer, highly rated models from top brands. That’s exactly why this deal on the critically praised Beats 360 headphones should be on your radar. They’re now down to $249 (originally $349.99) in Amazon’s early Black Friday sale.

With a design that looks like the love child of the AirPods Max and the Beats Studio Pro, these have an adjustable telescoping frame and a unique modular design that lets you mix and match ear pad colors. The color-swapping bundle isn’t currently on sale, but it’s reassuring to know you can replace the ear pads as they wear out.

They’re controlled by two buttons on each earcup and powered by a dedicated Beats chip, with support for both Android devices and iPhones. You can switch noise modes and, on an iPhone, activate features like Personalized Spatial Audio in Settings. They last up to 32 hours with ANC on, which is longer than both the more expensive Sony WH-1000XM6 and AirPods Max 2.

According to Beats, the 360 offer up to 1.75 times the noise cancellation of the Beats Studio Pro. PCMag’s review, which gave the headphones an “Excellent” rating, was impressed by how well they blocked out everything from plane engine noise to café chatter. The noise cancellation falls short of pricier models, and PCMag found the Sony WH-1000XM4C slightly better in that respect.

The PCMag review says the headphones deliver “nice, deep bass, reasonably crisp highs, and a more neutral tuning than you might expect for a pair of Beats headphones.” If you’re after long battery life, rich audio, and plush earcups you can swap for a pop of color, $249 is a great price for the Beats 360 headphones.

item.title: These Big Screen Hisense Mini-LED TVs Are up to 47% Off for Black Friday
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: substance, learning value

The entire Hisense U8 lineup is on sale for Black Friday, with prices starting at $749 for the 55-inch model (down from $1,424.99) and going up to $2,797.99 for the massive 100-inch version (originally $3,999.99). The discounts also extend to the 65-, 75-, and 85-inch models, with savings of up to $1,200 across the lineup. Regardless of which size you choose, Amazon throws in free delivery to the room of your choice, a service that normally costs $19.99.

Brightness is the U8QG’s main advantage, with the manufacturer estimating up to 5,000 nits of peak brightness, while PCMag measured around 3,200 nits when reviewing the 65-inch model. Actual performance will vary with the picture mode and content, but either figure points to strong highlights in Dolby Vision and HDR10 video. Its Mini-LED local dimming also produces deep blacks, although some light bloom can appear around bright objects on dark backgrounds. Audio-wise, its built-in 4.1.2-channel system, which includes surround channels, a subwoofer, and upward-firing speakers, gives movies more scale than typical TV speakers, though a separate sound system can still offer clearer separation and a broader soundstage.

The U8QG also has plenty to offer gamers using a current-generation console or a capable gaming PC. It supports refresh rates up to 165Hz, variable refresh rate, and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, with a measured 4.3 milliseconds of input lag at 1080p and 120Hz and 10.1 milliseconds at 4K and 60Hz. Those results should make controls feel responsive, even during fast-paced games. There’s also a side-mounted USB-C port that accepts DisplayPort video, while Google TV handles streaming alongside Apple AirPlay and Google Cast. The biggest inconvenience is the limited selection of three HDMI ports, since a console, soundbar, and streaming device would occupy all of them.

Black Friday FAQs

Does Amazon have Black Friday deals?

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

How long do Black Friday deals really last?

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Are Black Friday deals worth it?

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Why it is here: substance, learning value

Black Friday is here, and there are some substantial discounts on OLED gaming monitors from LG, Samsung, and ASUS, with savings ranging from $100 to nearly $580. And since OLED monitors generally offer near-instantaneous pixel response times, excellent contrast, and deep blacks, they're particularly appealing for games with fast movement or darker environments. The most affordable option is Samsung's 27-inch Odyssey OLED G6 at $409.99, while the biggest dollar discount goes to LG's 45-inch Ultragear at $1,121, down from $1,699.

These LG Ultragear monitors are up to 42% off

The 32-inch LG UltraGear 32GX870A-B is down to $829 from $1,399.99, saving you you 41% on a monitor that works well for both visually demanding games and competitive shooters. Its biggest advantage is LG's Dual Mode feature, which lets you switch between sharp 4K resolution at 240Hz and 1080p at 480Hz when faster gameplay takes priority. That makes it particularly versatile if you enjoy cinematic single-player games but also spend time playing competitive titles. That said, you'll need a powerful gaming PC to take full advantage of its higher refresh rates, particularly at 4K.

The 27-inch LG UltraGear 27GX790B-B is down to $668 from $999.99, a 33% discount. It’s built for speed, with a 1440p OLED panel that runs at 540Hz and a Dual Mode that pushes the refresh rate to 720Hz at 720p—making it particularly appealing for competitive games like Counter-Strike 2 or Valorant, where smooth motion and quick reactions are essential. Just keep in mind that you'll need a powerful PC capable of delivering exceptionally high frame rates to take full advantage of those refresh rates.

The 45-inch LG UltraGear 45GX900A-B is down to $980 from $1,699.99, a 42% discount. Its expansive 800R curved OLED display uses a 21:9 aspect ratio and 3440 x 1440 resolution, giving you a wider field of view that's particularly enjoyable for racing games, flight simulators, and cinematic adventures. You also get a 240Hz refresh rate, 0.03ms response time, and support for G-Sync and FreeSync Premium Pro.

Other OLED gaming monitors discounted for Black Friday

The 27-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G6 (G61SH) is down to $375 from $599.99, making it the most affordable OLED monitor in this roundup. Despite the lower price, you’re still getting a 1440p OLED panel with a 240Hz refresh rate and 0.03ms response time, which is more than enough for smooth gameplay in most modern titles.

The 27-inch Asus ROG Strix XG27ACDNG is a QD-OLED gaming monitor designed for fast-paced action, and it is currently down to $549 from $759. Its 1440p resolution and 360Hz refresh rate offer a good balance between sharp visuals and responsive gameplay, while the 0.03ms response time helps keep fast-moving objects clear. At this price, it's the more affordable alternative to the faster LG 27GX790B-B if you don't need refresh rates beyond 360Hz.

The least impressive deal is the 34-inch Alienware AW3425DW down to $712 from $799, saving you only 11% on the curved QD-OLED gaming monitor. Its 3440 x 1440 resolution and 21:9 aspect ratio give you more horizontal screen space for immersive games like racing simulators and open-world adventures, while the 240Hz refresh rate and 0.03ms response time help keep fast-moving action smooth and responsive. You also get FreeSync Premium Pro and G-Sync compatibility to help prevent screen tearing.

Black Friday FAQs

Does Amazon have Black Friday deals?

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Should I wait until Cyber Monday to shop online?

No. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. item.title: The Best Black Friday Deals on Smartwatches and Fitness Trackers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: average

Black Friday sales are now in full swing. I've been keeping an eye on all the best fitness trackers and smartwatch deals so that you can snag the best possible price from now until the end of Cyber Monday (Nov. 30). Whether you want a full-featured fitness smartwatch or a more recovery-focused tracker, here are the discounts you can find right now, including on brands like Apple, Oura, Garmin, and more.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is only $299 ($180 off)

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is a worthy competitor to the Oura Ring 5, with an included high-capacity charging case and no subscription. You can read Beth's comparison of the two here: most people would probably prefer the Oura, but the pros and cons are nuanced and you, dear reader, may be exactly the person the Ultrahuman is best for. The silver color is only $299 in this Black Friday deal, with other colors going for $379. The ring normally retails for $479, so that's $100 to $180 off, depending on color. That price includes a charging case and all the basic functionality of the ring; some extras require a subscription.

Pebble Watches are $25 off

This is a rare deal from Pebble! An email from the company states "We don’t do sales. Black Friday is the one exception each year." The Pebble Time 2 is on sale for $200, down from $225 regular price. This is the brand's rectangular watch, with a heart rate sensor, and an always-on MIP (e-paper) screen. The Pebble 2 Duo (a "do-over" version of the Pebble of yore) is also on sale, for $124, down from $149.

The Oura Ring 5 is only $299 ($100 off)

The Oura Ring 5 is at its lowest ever price: $299 for black and silver, $399 for all other colors. These are the lowest prices ever for these rings, which usually go for $399 and $499, respectively. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I've tried, although it's worth noting it requires a $5.99/month subscription fee.

For an even cheaper deal, the older Oura Ring 4 is $249—a full $100 off its list price of $349. If you opt for "stealth" (matte black), the price is $279; for gold, it's $286.61, down from $399. While this model has since been replaced by the Oura Ring 5, it's still an accurate and comfortable smart ring—especially if tracking your sleep is your priority.

Whoop bands are $40 off

Whoop may be one of the most expensive smart bands out there, thanks to its subscription-only model. But that price is particularly low right now, since the Peak membership that normally goes for $239 is now $199. Peak is the middle tier, and it's the one Beth recommends. While you can get Whoop One for $189 in this sale, the $10 you save isn't really worth it given the features you'd be missing. We also wouldn't normally recommend Whoop Life, since its ECG readings and blood pressure estimates aren't really worth the extra cost. That said, if you do want it, the Life tier is $299 right now instead of $359.

The Luna Band is 20% off

The new Luna band is on sale for $119.20, down from a normal price of $149. The Luna band is made by Indian smartwatch company Noise, the same company behind the Luna Ring that Beth reviewed last year. The ring is no longer available in the U.S., but the band is. It's a Whoop-style screenless fitness tracker, potentially a worthy competitor to the Fitbit Air and other smart bands.

This is the brand-new Apple Watch model, and it's actually worth the upgrade. item.title: I Tried Coros' New 'Expedition-Focused' Smartwatch, and I'm Impressed
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: average

Coros has unveiled the Vertix 4, an “expedition-focused” update to the Vertix 2 and 2S. Coros says it pairs the brand's brightest display yet with long battery life, and after unboxing it myself, I can definitely say it has a more refined feel that could indeed suit the office as well as the summit.

This watch is being marketed as a major step up from the Vertix 2S, with an AMOLED display, a more refined design, satellite maps and, for the first time on a Coros watch, a built-in flashlight. The Vertix 4 will be available to buy starting on Black Friday, Nov. 27, but it won't exactly be at a discount: It costs $799, a $100 increase over the Vertix 2S.

That price does still undercut the latest Garmin Fenix 9 line-up, which starts at $999, though some rivals are cheaper still. For instance, the Suunto Vertical 2 steel model costs $599, and the Garmin Fenix 8 is currently on sale for $749.99 at Amazon.

I've only just started testing the Vertix 4 and haven't even had enough time to get through its substantial battery life, but I can share some first impressions, particularly in how it compares with the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro that launched earlier this year.

The first Coros watch with a flashlight

Built-in flashlights have become a must-have feature on premium sports watches, and now the Vertix 4 is the first Coros watch to get one. Coros has departed from the usual layout, though. Garmin, Suunto and Amazfit put the light on top of the watch, but Coros places it on the side, between the digital dial and the back button.

A vibrant AMOLED display

Previous Vertix watches used a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display. MIP has advantages, most notably longer battery life, but I know I much prefer the vibrant display on AMOLED screens, like on the Vertix 4. It is the biggest visual change and a large part of why the watch looks more premium than its predecessors.

Up to a month of battery life and two days of multi-band GPS

Coros claims up to 30 days in watch mode, or 10 days with the screen always on. It also quotes 48 hours of multi-band GPS tracking with the screen always on. I haven't had time to test these claims properly, so stay tuned.

A sports watch first, a smartwatch second

Coros watches are high-quality sports watches, but don't expect to find all the little lifestyle features you've come to expect on a more traditional smartwatch:

- Music: It can store tracks, but only files you drag and drop onto the watch. It doesn't pair with streaming services.

- Payments: There is no NFC payment support.

- Watch faces: Customization is more limited than on rivals.

On paper, the Vertix 4 looks like a significant upgrade: a better display, a more attractive design, a flashlight and satellite maps, at a price well below the Fenix 9 line-up. The $100 increase and cheaper alternatives like the Suunto Vertical 2 and discounted Fenix 8 will matter to some buyers, as will the limited smart features.
